articles.title: P53's five-hour rhythm may let resonance target gene networks on command
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: Can networks of genes be stimulated using resonance? Researchers at the Niels Bohr Institute are investigating whether the protein p53, which activates a range of different genes, can be induced to communicate with the body's cells "on command." Perhaps resonance is the key to stimulating the body toward a new form of self-healing?

articles.title: New methods make tracking individual bird species during migration possible
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: Researchers at Cornell Lab of Ornithology, University of Massachusetts and University of Illinois have developed breakthrough methods to track the migration of individual bird species by combining participatory science data with weather radar technology. This advancement addresses a long-standing limitation in migration monitoring: While radar can detect birds in flight, it cannot identify which species are migrating.

articles.title: Scientists mapped every neural connection in a fruit fly and found a surprise
articles.summary: A groundbreaking new connectome maps every neural connection in an adult fruit fly’s central nervous system, creating an unprecedented view of how the brain and body work together. The findings suggest that complex behaviors emerge from distributed local circuits rather than a single central controller, offering new clues about intelligence, movement, and brain function.

articles.title: Popular joint supplement glucosamine linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
articles.summary: A major study suggests glucosamine, a popular supplement for joint pain, could be linked to faster progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers found a 25% higher likelihood of developing dementia among glucosamine users and uncovered biological clues that may explain why.

articles.title: Earth's first animals barely evolved until sex changed everything
articles.summary: Earth’s earliest animals may have held evolution back because they reproduced asexually, creating low-competition communities that changed very little over time. When environmental pressures pushed them toward sexual reproduction, biodiversity exploded and evolution accelerated dramatically.
